assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory gave the first controllable, non-perturbative framework for strongly correlated electrons, exact in infinite dimensions and, combined with electronic-structure methods (DFT+DMFT), usable for real materials. It explains the Mott transition, the coexistence of Hubbard bands and quasiparticles, and correlated-metal spectra, and it changed how calculated and measured spectra are compared. I judge it original, clear and of lasting impact, and I note that it is close to my own working field.
assessment.attribution: The infinite-dimensional limit and the self-consistent mapping onto an impurity problem are usually credited to Metzner and Vollhardt and to Georges and Kotliar, with Müller-Hartmann and Jarrell among others contributing; Kotliar also led the DFT+DMFT merger. The three supplied names form a defensible configuration, but the omission of Metzner is a real fairness concern that I cannot resolve from the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: More than three decades of use, validated against many oxides, heavy-fermion systems and cold-atom simulators, and now a standard tool in condensed-matter theory. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Whether Metzner and Müller-Hartmann deserve recognition alongside the three credited names is unresolved.
Known limits of DMFT (neglect of non-local correlations) mean cluster extensions may be viewed as the more mature successors; I have not verified details of the original priority claims.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 classification of time-reversal-invariant insulators opened the topological-materials field, linking band structure to protected edge and surface states. It is original, conceptually clean, and now touches spintronics, photonics, cold atoms and quantum computing proposals.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical contribution. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the Molenkamp-group HgTe observation (2007) were key to confirmation; the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Zhang contributions are not in this credit list. The three-person split theory/theory/experiment is plausible, but the allocation relative to the supplied alternatives is not fully settled.
assessment.maturity: Strong, independent experimental confirmation in HgTe wells, Bi-based and Bi2Se3-class materials with ARPES, plus an extensive follow-on literature. Mature and timely, though the 2016 prize already recognised topological phases.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2016 prize on topological phases may weigh against a second topological award.
The omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang from the supplied names leaves credit allocation contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene, followed by observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity, created a new experimental platform for strongly correlated and topological physics in moire materials. The theory is built on continuum band-structure modelling of the sort I know well, and the interplay of prediction and experiment is exemplary.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald gave the 2011 flat-band prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group delivered the 2018 experimental breakthrough. The three names map naturally onto the theory/experiment division, though Cory Dean, Philip Kim and other experimental groups also played major roles in the broader moire field.
assessment.maturity: The field is only about eight years old, with many open questions about the superconducting mechanism and sample-dependent behaviour. Reproducibility across groups is good for the basic phases, but the interpretation is still evolving. Timely but somewhat early.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism and ground states are debated.
Credit to other experimental groups and to early twisted-bilayer theory is not captured in the supplied list.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions, and later giant TMR in MgO barriers, is a spin-dependent transport effect with direct impact on read heads and non-volatile magnetic memory. It is a magnetism problem where electronic-structure theory of spin-polarized tunnelling and interfacial coherence has played a major part.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera reported the room-temperature effect in 1995; Parkin and Yuasa/Djayaprawira groups achieved the giant MgO-based results in 2004. The supplied set includes Parkin but not Yuasa or Djayaprawira, and I am unsure whether the MgO breakthrough is correctly assigned. Julliere's earlier low-temperature work is also relevant.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature and technologically deployed, with decades of independent confirmation. However, the 2007 prize for GMR covers closely related ground and the committee may see this as incremental.
uncertainties: Attribution for the MgO coherent-tunnelling step is uncertain with these three names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, reached fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and underpins redefinition of the second, tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy. It is original, practical and cleanly attributable.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated the early strontium clocks; Ye's group made the leading accuracy and stability demonstrations. A two-person prize is coherent, although other groups (Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, others) also contributed; the supplied names exclude them.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many independent laboratories and approaching adoption in international timekeeping. The timing is good, though the 2005 and 2012 prizes also honoured precision spectroscopy and ion control.
uncertainties: The relative role of Hall and Hänsch in frequency combs, already honoured in 2005, versus lattice-clock-specific contributions.
Whether the committee views the work as closely related to previously awarded precision-measurement prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Discovery of superconductivity at 26 K in LaFeAsO(1-x)Fx, then up to 55 K in related compounds, established a second family of high-temperature superconductors that clearly contradicted the notion that cuprates were unique. It also sharpened the debate over multiband pairing. The discovery was unexpected and important.
assessment.attribution: A single, clearly identified discoverer of the 2008 first report, which makes a single-laureate prize easy to configure. Subsequent increases in Tc by Chinese groups (Ren, Chen, Wang) were built on the discovery and might be seen as contributing, but these names are not in the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed within weeks and extensively studied. After about eighteen years, there is still no consensus pairing mechanism and no practical application at scale, so the impact is more scientific than technological.
uncertainties: Absence of a settled pairing theory makes the lasting interpretation unclear.
Contributions of the groups that raised Tc quickly are not reflected in the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultrasoft pseudopotentials, the PAW method and their efficient plane-wave implementations are the working machinery behind most modern first-principles calculations of solids. Their impact on materials physics, chemistry and the reproducibility of DFT results is very large. I declare my own proximity to this community and have tried to weigh the case fairly rather than favour it.
assessment.attribution: Vanderbilt (ultrasoft pseudopotentials), Blöchl (PAW) and Kresse (the implementation in VASP and the PAW adaptation with Joubert) are plausible choices; norm-conserving pseudopotentials (Hamann, Schlüter, Chiang), Car-Parrinello and other methods are also relevant. Whether a prize for a method of this kind is appropriate for physics is also a question, given the 1998 chemistry prize for DFT.
assessment.maturity: Mature, ubiquitous and verified through multi-code reproducibility studies. Recognition is timely if the committee accepts computational methods as prize-worthy.
uncertainties: Whether computational methodology fits the prize criteria, and the precedent set by the 1998 DFT recognition.
Credit among the many pseudopotential and plane-wave developers is crowded.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 1995 proposal for quantum gates with laser-cooled trapped ions, and the later proposals for quantum simulation with cold atoms, were foundational for quantum information platforms. The work is theoretical, concrete and has been implemented experimentally on several platforms.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are the clear proposers of the ion-trap gate and of several related schemes. A two-theorist prize is coherent; experimental realisation by Wineland's and Blatt's groups is a separate matter, and Wineland was honoured in 2012.
assessment.maturity: The scheme has been realised, and scalable ion-trap quantum computers are being built. The long-term role of trapped ions in quantum computing is still developing, so recognition may be somewhat early for the computing claim but is secure for the proposal itself.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize on controlling single quantum systems.
Distinguishing the ion-trap contribution from the separate optical-lattice work credited elsewhere.
